query: For a FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy used as a thin coating on a conventional metal substrate, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs overall wear resistance and microscopic deformation during sliding in the intended high-temperature operating regime? Define a controlled change relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the corresponding directional changes in wear and deformation, state the regime in which those predictions should hold, identify supporting prior evidence, and specify a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In FeNiCrCoCu HEA thin coatings, reducing the initial grain size by controlled annealing promotes dynamic amorphization during high-temperature sliding. This leads to the formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer that localizes shear into high-angle grain boundaries, thereby reducing wear and moderating microscopic deformation compared to a coarse-grained baseline.
generation.material_initial_state: FeNiCrCoCu HEA thin coating with a relatively coarse grain structure (baseline condition).
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled annealing treatment (or other thermal processing) to refine the grain size prior to or after deposition.
generation.conditions: High-temperature sliding regime in an inert or non-oxidizing environment (conditions similar to those under which dynamic amorphization was observed in comparable HEAs).
generation.structural_mediator: Grain size, specifically the formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer via dynamic amorphization.
generation.mechanism: A refined grain structure is more susceptible to dynamic amorphization during sliding, where localized shear at high-angle grain boundaries forms an ultra-nanocrystalline layer that confines deformation and reduces wear. This mechanism, resembling the inverse Hall-Petch behavior observed in other HEAs, limits the propagation of plastic damage.
generation.predicted_outcome: The annealed (grain-refined) coating is expected to show lower wear rates and different microscopic deformation patterns (e.g., shallower, more localized deformation zones with lower friction coefficients) relative to the baseline coarse-grained coating.
generation.baseline: Coating produced without the annealing treatment (coarse grain size), expected to be less capable of forming the protective ultra-nanocrystalline layer under high-temperature sliding.
generation.boundary: These predictions are anticipated to hold specifically under high-temperature, inert (non-oxidizing) conditions. In oxidizing atmospheres or at temperatures significantly deviating from the operational regime, the mechanism may differ.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative relationship between grain size reduction and the wear/deformation improvements is uncertain, and the influence of Cu in this HEA compared to other alloys (like CoCrFeMnNi) might modify the dynamic amorphization response.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of FeNiCrCoCu coating samples: one set with the baseline (coarse-grained) deposition process and another set with a controlled annealing treatment to refine the grain size. Subject both sets to high-temperature sliding wear tests in an inert atmosphere. Post-test, analyze the samples for wear rates, friction coefficients, and microstructural changes (e.g., grain size distribution and evidence of dynamic amorphization within the near-surface layer) using techniques such as TEM or STEM.
measurements: Microstructural evidence for the presence of an ultra-nanocrystalline layer/dynamic amorphization
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if the grain-refined (annealed) samples do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in wear rate or if they fail to develop an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer during wear testing. Similarly, if the microscopic deformation behavior (e.g., shear localization or friction response) of the grain-refined samples is equivalent to or worse than that of the baseline samples under identical high-temperature, inert conditions, the hypothesis is not supported.

cited_evidence.text:
Evidence of Inverse Hall-Petch Behavior and Low Friction and Wear in High Entropy Alloys

Abstract: AbstractWe present evidence of inverse Hall-Petch behavior for a single-phase high entropy alloy (CoCrFeMnNi) in ultra-high vacuum and show that it is associated with low friction coefficients (~0.3). Grain size measurements by STEM validate a recently proposed dynamic amorphization model that accurately predicts grain size-dependent shear strength in the inverse Hall-Petch regime. Wear rates in the initially soft (coarse grained) material were shown to be remarkably low (~10–6 mm3/N-m), the lowest for any HEA tested in an inert environment where oxidation and the formation of mixed metal-oxide films is mitigated. The combined high wear resistance and low friction are linked to the formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer. The dynamic amorphization model was also used to predict an average high angle grain boundary energy (0.87 J/m2). This value was used to explain cavitation-induced nanoporosity found in the highly deformed surface layer, a phenomenon that has been linked to superplasticity.Subject terms: Structural materials, Structural properties
